title: Why the Orthodox Church does not receive the Council of Florence
subtitle: A synod becomes a Council when the whole Church recognises her own faith in it.
summary: The Council of Ferrara-Florence (1438-1439) published a decree of union that the Orthodox Church has never received. The reason is ecclesiological before it is polemical: a council is not made a Council by its convocation, its attendance, or its signatures, but by the Church recognising in it the faith she already holds. The Symbol had been closed by Ephesus and Chalcedon; the consent given at Florence was given under financial and political duress; Mark of Ephesus did not sign; and within decades the Eastern sees, the Church of Rus, and finally Constantinople itself set the union aside. Vincent of Lerins, Athanasius, Jerome, Gregory the Great, and the precedent of Ariminum supply the rule by which the Church judged it.

essay.text: Most people meet the Council of Florence as a piece of ammunition in an argument. That is not where it belongs. It belongs to a question every Christian eventually has to answer for himself: how do I know that what my Church teaches me is the faith of the apostles, and not the settlement of a committee that met under pressure? Florence is that question in its sharpest form. A council was convened. An emperor and a pope were present. Bishops of East and West sat together for more than a year. A decree of union was signed and published, with an overwhelming majority of the Greek delegation subscribing. And the Orthodox Church does not receive it. Understanding why is not a matter of scoring against Rome. It is a matter of learning how the Church recognises her own voice.
How the Church recognises a Council

An Ecumenical Council is not made by its convocation, its attendance, or its paperwork. It is made by the Holy Spirit speaking in the Church, and the Church knows that voice by receiving it. Vincent of Lerins gave the working rule in the fifth century: hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all, and test it by universality, antiquity, and consent. Pope Gregory the Great, writing to the patriarchs of the East, says that he receives and reveres the four Councils as he does the four books of the Gospel, and he names them one by one. The councils he lists are the ones the whole Church had already taken into her prayer and her preaching. Reception is not a vote taken afterwards, and it is not a majority. It is the Church over time recognising, or failing to recognise, her own faith in what was written. A synod that the Church does not receive is not a Council whose enforcement failed. It was never a Council.
Ariminum, the council that was never received

This is not an argument invented for Florence. In 359 the Emperor Constantius assembled at Ariminum a synod far larger than Nicaea, some four hundred bishops of the West, and kept them there until they subscribed a formula that abandoned the word by which Nicaea had confessed the Son. They signed. Jerome describes what followed in a sentence the Church has never forgotten: the whole world groaned, and was astonished to find itself Arian. Athanasius, writing with the ninety bishops of Egypt and Libya to men who wanted Ariminum preferred to Nicaea, answers that the word of the Lord which came through the ecumenical Synod at Nicaea abides forever. Numbers did not save Ariminum. Imperial backing did not save it. The Church did not receive it, and it fell away. Something like it had happened again at Ephesus in 449, the assembly we call the Robber Council. Two years later at Chalcedon, when the leaders of that assembly stood to be deposed for what had been done to Flavian, the bishops of Illyricum, who had themselves subscribed in 449, answered simply, we all have erred, let us all be pardoned. Bishops can go wrong together, and the Church corrects them. That is not an embarrassment in Orthodox ecclesiology. It is Orthodox ecclesiology.
What Florence decided, and what had already been closed

The council opened at Ferrara in 1438, moved to Florence in 1439, and published its decree of union, Laetentur Caeli, on 6 July 1439. It settled four things in Rome's favour: that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son as from one principle and by a single spiration; that souls not fully purified are cleansed after death by punishments; that the Eucharist may be consecrated in unleavened as well as leavened bread; and that the Roman Pontiff holds primacy over the whole world, is the successor of Peter, and is the true vicar of Christ, head of the whole Church, father and teacher of all Christians. The first of these was the hinge, and the Orthodox objection to it has two parts that must not be collapsed into one. The first is dogmatic. In the faith the Church received, the Father alone is cause and source within the Godhead, and the Spirit has his existence from the Father. To name the Father and the Son together as one principle of the Spirit's existence is, in our judgement, to give the Son what belongs to the Father alone. It should be said plainly that the Latin tradition denies that its formula means this: it holds that the Son has his part in the spiration from the Father, so that the Father remains the one fountain and no second source is introduced. Orthodox theology has not been persuaded that this saves the point, because what is at issue is not the number of sources but which Person is cause. That is a real disagreement, and it deserves to be stated as a disagreement rather than as a caricature. The second objection is canonical, and it does not depend on settling the first. The Symbol was closed. Ephesus forbade any man to bring forward, or to write, or to compose a different Faith as a rival to the one established at Nicaea, and Chalcedon repeated the prohibition inside its own Definition. A see that adds a clause to a conciliar Symbol, and then convenes a council to require the addition of everyone else, has not developed the faith. It has legislated over a text that was never its own.
The conditions under which men consented

None of this would matter if the East had freely recognised its own faith in the decree. It did not, and the circumstances make that intelligible. Constantinople was a city waiting for a siege. The Ottoman advance had reduced the empire to little more than its capital, and the Emperor John VIII went to Italy because Western arms were the only help left. The Greek delegation travelled at papal expense and lived on a papal allowance. The nineteenth-century history of the council translated by Basil Popoff records that the Pope found the allowance the best way of making the Greeks obedient: when they would not comply their pay was stopped, so that many of the bishops were obliged to sell their clothes, and when they agreed their wages were given out at once as a reward for obedience. Patriarch Joseph II, who had said that he would sooner suffer any pain than turn traitor to what had been received from the Ecumenical Councils, and that he and his would be martyrs in deed or martyrs in will, did not hold. He died in Florence on 10 June 1439, before the decree was signed. Of the Eastern bishops who remained to the end, Mark of Ephesus alone did not sign. Duress does not make a false teaching true, and it does not make a true teaching false. But it does explain why those signatures were never the consent of the Eastern Church. They were the consent of exhausted men a long way from home, who had been given a reason to sign that had nothing to do with the Holy Spirit.
The answer of the Churches, and how we hold it

The answer came slowly, and from every direction. Signatories repudiated their signatures on reaching home. The Patriarchs of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem met at Jerusalem in 1443 and rejected the union. In Rus, Metropolitan Isidore returned from Florence a cardinal, proclaimed the union in Moscow, and was arrested; the Russian Church elected its own metropolitan in 1448, and Moscow afterwards dated its independence from its refusal of Florence. In Constantinople the union was proclaimed in Hagia Sophia in December 1452, and the people largely stayed away. What the union failed to win was not the argument of the theologians but the recognition of the faithful, and that is the only thing that could have made it a Council. In 1484 a synod at Constantinople under Patriarch Symeon formally set the union aside and prescribed how Latins were to be received. As for the help the union was meant to buy, the crusade that followed was destroyed at Varna in 1444, and what reached the City in 1453 was a few hundred men. Constantinople fell on 29 May 1453. That is the part to carry away. Florence is not a trophy for us. It is the record of what happens when a Church in real terror is offered survival at the price of a clause, and a warning that the price is always presented as small. The faith is not ours to trade, not for armies, not for peace, not even for the ending of a schism we genuinely grieve. We do not receive the Council of Florence because the Church did not receive it, and the Church did not receive it because she did not hear in it the voice of her Lord.

florilegium.author: St Vincent of Lerins
florilegium.text: Moreover, in the Catholic Church itself, all possible care must be taken, that we hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all. For that is truly and in the strictest sense Catholic, which, as the name itself and the reason of the thing declare, comprehends all universally. This rule we shall observe if we follow universality, antiquity, consent. We shall follow universality if we confess that one faith to be true, which the whole Church throughout the world confesses; antiquity, if we in no wise depart from those interpretations which it is manifest were notoriously held by our holy ancestors and fathers; consent, in like manner, if in antiquity itself we adhere to the consentient definitions and determinations of all, or at the least of almost all priests and doctors.
florilegium.gloss: The rule by which the Church judges any synod. Florence fails all three tests at once: it is not what the whole Church confesses, it is not what the fathers held, and it never obtained the consent of the Eastern sees whose delegates subscribed it.

florilegium.author: Pope St Gregory the Great
florilegium.work: Registrum Epistolarum, Book I, Letter 25, to John of Constantinople and the other Patriarchs
florilegium.text: I confess that I receive and revere, as the four books of the Gospel so also the four Councils: to wit, the Nicene, in which the perverse doctrine of Arius is overthrown; the Constantinopolitan also, in which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius is refuted; further, the first Ephesine, in which the impiety of Nestorius is condemned; and the Chalcedonian, in which the pravity of Eutyches and Dioscorus is reprobated.
florilegium.gloss: A Bishop of Rome states the criterion plainly: the Councils he venerates are the ones already received and confessed by the whole Church, named one by one. Authority follows reception; it does not substitute for it.

florilegium.author: St Athanasius the Great
florilegium.reference: §1 (NPNF Second Series, vol. 4), the letter of the ninety bishops of Egypt and Libya
florilegium.text: But the word of the Lord which came through the ecumenical Synod at Nicæa, abides forever.
florilegium.gloss: Athanasius and the ninety bishops of Egypt and Libya set the permanence of what Nicaea confessed against every later assembly that would revise it.

florilegium.author: St Athanasius the Great
florilegium.text: But since we have heard that certain wishing to oppose it are attempting to cite a synod supposed to have been held at Ariminum, and are eagerly striving that it should prevail rather than the other, we think it right to write and put you in mind, not to endure anything of the sort.
florilegium.gloss: The standing precedent. Ariminum (359) was larger than Nicaea and had the emperor behind it. Athanasius does not argue about its procedure; he tells the Churches not to receive it. That is the same act the East performed after 1439.

florilegium.author: St Jerome of Stridon
florilegium.text: At that moment the term Usia was abolished: the Nicene Faith stood condemned by acclamation. The whole world groaned, and was astonished to find itself Arian.
florilegium.gloss: Jerome on the aftermath of Ariminum. A council can be signed by nearly everybody and still not be the faith. The groan is the sound of a Church that has not received what her bishops subscribed.

florilegium.author: The Third Ecumenical Council, Ephesus
florilegium.work: Canons of the Council of Ephesus
florilegium.text: When these things had been read, the holy Synod decreed that it is unlawful for any man to bring forward, or to write, or to compose a different (ἑτέραν) Faith as a rival to that established by the holy Fathers assembled with the Holy Ghost in Nicæa. But those who shall dare to compose a different faith, or to introduce or offer it to persons desiring to turn to the acknowledgment of the truth, whether from Heathenism or from Judaism, or from any heresy whatsoever, shall be deposed, if they be bishops or clergymen; bishops from the episcopate and clergymen from the clergy; and if they be laymen, they shall be anathematized.
florilegium.gloss: The Symbol was closed by an Ecumenical Council a thousand years before Florence. The question at Florence was therefore never only whether the addition was true, but whether anyone was competent to make it.

florilegium.author: The Fourth Ecumenical Council, Chalcedon
florilegium.text: These things, therefore, having been expressed by us with the greatest accuracy and attention, the holy Ecumenical Synod defines that no one shall be suffered to bring forward a different faith (ἑτέραν πίστιν), nor to write, nor to put together, nor to excogitate, nor to teach it to others.
florilegium.gloss: Chalcedon writes the prohibition into the body of its own Definition. The two Councils that gave the Church her Christology also fixed the form of her Symbol.

florilegium.author: The Fourth Ecumenical Council, Chalcedon
florilegium.reference: Session I, the response of the bishops of Illyricum (NPNF Second Series, vol. 14)
florilegium.text: We all have erred, let us all be pardoned.
florilegium.gloss: Spoken at Chalcedon when the judges proposed that Dioscorus and the leaders of the assembly of 449 suffer what they had inflicted on Flavian. The Illyrian bishops, who had themselves subscribed in 449, ask instead for a general pardon. An episcopate can subscribe together and repent together. The Church is not bound by a signature she never recognised.

florilegium.author: Ivan N. Ostroumoff
florilegium.work: The History of the Council of Florence, translated by Basil Popoff, edited by J. M. Neale (Joseph Masters, 1861)
florilegium.reference: p. 34, on the Patriarch Joseph II before the council
florilegium.text: If even the Latins force us to something, we will always keep to the sound doctrine of the Fathers. Let them threaten us with tortures; we will sooner suffer any pain than turn traitors to anything received by us from the Œcumenical Councils and the holy teachers of the Church: we will either be martyrs in deed, or martyrs in will.
florilegium.gloss: The Patriarch of Constantinople on the eve of the council. The same page describes him as old, weak, and undecided, and says that time proved him false to his own words. He died at Florence before the decree was signed. Historical testimony from a nineteenth-century Orthodox historian, not a patristic text.

florilegium.author: Ivan N. Ostroumoff
florilegium.work: The History of the Council of Florence, translated by Basil Popoff, edited by J. M. Neale (Joseph Masters, 1861)
florilegium.reference: p. 42, on the delegation at Ferrara
florilegium.text: The Pope found this the best way of making the Greeks obedient. For whenever the Greeks refused to comply with any of his wishes, he immediately stopped their pay, so that many of the Bishops were obliged to sell their clothes. But as soon as the Greeks agreed to his proposals, their wages were immediately given out as a sort of reward for their obedience.
florilegium.gloss: The material conditions under which the Eastern delegation deliberated. Consent purchased by an allowance is not the consent of a Church. Historical testimony from a nineteenth-century Orthodox historian, not a patristic text.

scripture.note: For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us. The apostolic pattern: the decision is taken by the assembly with the whole Church, and it is then sent out to be received.
The sheep follow him, for they know his voice, and the next verse adds that a stranger they will not follow. Reception is nothing more dramatic than this, and nothing less.
Though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed. No office in the Church exempts a teaching from the test.
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust. The deposit is guarded, not renegotiated under pressure.
Stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.
Remove not the old landmarks, which thy fathers placed, the verse the Fathers apply to the Symbol of Faith.

modernScholarship.work: A. Edward Siecienski, The Filioque: History of a Doctrinal Controversy (Oxford University Press)
modernScholarship.usedFor: The spine of the source thread. Behind the thread's account of ninth-century Roman refusal to add the clause to the Creed, the silver shields of Leo III, the transmission of Maximus' Letter to Marinus through Anastasius Bibliothecarius, the Carolingian promotion of the Filioque at Frankfurt and Aachen, and the theology of Patriarch John XI Bekkos. Nothing from it is quoted, and after this review pass nothing drawn from it is asserted in the essay either: the one claim that had survived drafting, that an older Latin defence read the Western phrase as manifestation and mission rather than origin and that Florence set that defence aside, has been cut from the essay body because it could not be verified from a public-domain source in this session.

modernScholarship.work: Joseph Gill, The Council of Florence (Cambridge University Press)
modernScholarship.usedFor: The standard modern narrative of the sessions and negotiations, and the chronology used to sanity-check dates. Note for the reviewer: the source thread attributes the passage about the Greeks' pay being stopped to Gill, but that exact English wording belongs to the 1861 Popoff translation of Ostroumoff, which is public domain and is therefore quoted directly in the florilegium instead. Gill is also the reason the disputed 1450 synod is left out.

The judgement that only a very small part of the Byzantine clergy and people ever accepted the decrees, that many signatories revoked at home, and that the political situation made dispassionate theological discussion nearly impossible. Restated in our own words, never quoted. His English rendering of the Notaras saying was the wording the source thread used, and every trace of it has now been removed from this study.

modernScholarship.work: Deno J. Geanakoplos, 'The Council of Florence and the Problem of Union between the Greek and Latin Churches', Church History
modernScholarship.usedFor: The political framing: union as an instrument of jurisdiction for the papacy and of survival for the emperors, and the identification of papal supremacy rather than the Filioque as the article with the widest practical consequences for the Greeks.

modernScholarship.work: Metropolitan Hilarion Alfeyev, 'The Reception of the Ecumenical Councils in the Early Church'
modernScholarship.usedFor: The reception criterion, and the chronology of the Eastern rejections after 1439 (Rus, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem, Constantinople). Dates taken from it are flagged in the editorial notes, because they do not all match the standard reference works.

modernScholarship.work: Francis Dvornik, Byzantine Missions Among the Slavs
modernScholarship.usedFor: That ninth-century Rome still recited the Creed without the addition and that the popes of that period did not approve the interpolation. Background only; no claim from it appears in the essay text.

modernScholarship.work: Agnes Kriza, Depicting Orthodoxy in the Russian Middle Ages: The Novgorod Icon of Sophia
modernScholarship.usedFor: The place of the refusal of Florence in Muscovite self-understanding and in the Moscow metropolitanate's movement toward autocephaly in 1448.

modernScholarship.work: Simon Malmenvall, '(Mis)trusting Unification: Examples of East Slavic Perception of the Council of Florence'
modernScholarship.usedFor: East Slavic reception of the union, the polemical Rus' accounts of Metropolitan Isidore, and the shift of symbolic centre from Kyiv to Moscow.

modernScholarship.work: Sylvester Syropoulos, Memoirs, in V. Laurent's critical edition and in modern translation
modernScholarship.usedFor: The eyewitness detail that the representative of the Patriarch of Antioch carried written instructions not to consent to any addition or subtraction. Syropoulos is a fifteenth-century primary source, but the edition and translation available are modern and in copyright, so nothing from it is quoted and the detail is not asserted in the essay.

modernScholarship.work: Ivan N. Ostroumoff, The History of the Council of Florence, Holy Transfiguration Monastery edition (Boston, 1971)
modernScholarship.usedFor: The edition the source thread cites by page number. This draft quotes instead the underlying 1861 translation by Basil Popoff, edited by J. M. Neale, which is public domain and is on archive.org. The thread's page numbers (34, 58, 85, 154, 188) belong to the 1971 reprint and do not correspond to the 1861 pagination; the two passages quoted here were located at pp. 34 and 42 of the 1861 scan.

modernScholarship.work: Andrew of Santa Croce, Acts of the Council of Florence, and Bessarion, To Alexius Lascaris, and Bl. John Eugenikos, Against the Council of Florence, as cited in the source thread
modernScholarship.usedFor: Fifteenth-century primary sources quoted in the thread through modern editions and translations. Not used or quoted in this draft; if the reviewer wants them, a public-domain edition has to be located first.

modernScholarship.work: Bartholomew de Barberiis, Theological Course according to the Mind of the Seraphic Doctor, as cited in the source thread
modernScholarship.usedFor: A Latin scholastic defence of the Florentine position that the thread quoted in modern English translation. Not used, not quoted, and not characterised in the essay.

editorialNotes: VERIFICATION PASS, what I actually did. All ten florilegium entries were fetched from their source URL in this review session and checked word by word. All ten passed and all ten are kept. Nothing was invented, nothing was reconstructed from memory, and no entry was deleted for failing verification. Specifics: Vincent, Commonitory II.6 on newadvent 3506, exact. Gregory the Great, Registrum I.25 on newadvent 360201025, exact, and the page confirms the recipients are John of Constantinople with Eulogius of Alexandria, Gregory of Antioch, John of Jerusalem and Anastasius. Athanasius, Ad Afros §1 on newadvent 2819, both sentences exact, including the full continuation of the Ariminum sentence through 'not to endure anything of the sort'. Jerome, Against the Luciferians §19 on newadvent 3005, exact, and the sentence does begin 'At that moment the term Usia was abolished', not 'Then'. Ephesus Canon VII on newadvent 3810, exact. Chalcedon Definition and the Illyrian acclamation both on newadvent 3811, exact. Ostroumoff, both passages found in the 1861 archive.org scan.

CORRECTIONS I MADE TO THE FLORILEGIUM. (1) The Ephesus Canon VII entry was missing the parenthetical Greek that newadvent prints, 'a different (ἑτέραν) Faith'. Restored. The old editorial note claimed the draft reproduced newadvent exactly including the Greek; it did not. (2) The Chalcedon Definition was likewise missing '(ἑτέραν πίστιν)'. Restored, and the reference now names Session V, which is where the page puts it. (3) The Chalcedon Session I entry carried a gloss that placed the Illyrian words loosely 'on the assembly of 449'. The page shows the immediate occasion is the judges' proposal that Dioscorus and the leaders of 449 suffer what they inflicted on Flavian. Gloss corrected, and the reference now names the Illyrian bishops. (4) Both Ostroumoff references now carry real page numbers from the 1861 scan, p. 34 and p. 42, instead of approximate chapter guesses. (5) The pay passage now opens with the preceding sentence, 'The Pope found this the best way of making the Greeks obedient', which is verified and which supplies the antecedent for 'his' and 'he'. Without it the quotation floats free of its subject. Please still confirm both Greek parentheticals against the page image, since my fetches were mediated.

BROKEN LINK REMOVED. The draft carried saintSlug 'jerome-of-stridon'. There is no such directory in data/saints (85 saints, none for Jerome), so that field would have produced a dead link. Removed. saintSlug 'athanasius-the-great' is real and is kept. Note that data/saints/mark-of-ephesus DOES exist, so the study can link to St Mark's saint page even though no quotable text of his is available.

SCRIPTURE EDITION MISMATCH, corrected. The draft's Proverbs 22:28 note quoted the KJV, 'Remove not the ancient landmark which thy fathers have set'. The app ships Proverbs from Brenton (data/bible/proverbs/22.json, source brenton-lxx-pd), which reads 'Remove not the old landmarks, which thy fathers placed'. A reader tapping through would have seen different words from the ones the note quoted, which editorial-standards.md forbids ('never mix editions silently'). The note now uses the Brenton wording. All five New Testament notes were checked against the app's own KJV files and now match them, including the 'For it seemed good' opening of Acts 15:28 and 'Stand fast, and hold the traditions' at 2 Thessalonians 2:15.

SCRIPTURE VERSE MISATTRIBUTION, corrected. The draft attached 'a stranger will they not follow' to John 10:4. In the app's KJV that clause is John 10:5. The note now attributes each half to the right verse.

COPYRIGHT: THE NOTARAS SAYING IS GONE. The draft's essay reported the saying in reworded form and its editorial notes reproduced the copyrighted English wording verbatim. Both are removed. Reasons, in order: the familiar English sentence belongs to a modern copyrighted translation and reproducing it anywhere in the deliverable, including a note to the reviewer, is the thing we are not allowed to do; the sentence carried no ecclesiological weight the paragraph did not already have; and the drafter's own note conceded it was the closest the study came to point-scoring. The paragraph now states the substance that matters, that the union failed to win the recognition of the faithful. If the reviewer wants Notaras back, it needs a public-domain rendering of Doukas located first, plus a decision about whether we want to publish it at all.

COPYRIGHT SCAN, result. I read the essay and every gloss against the source thread's block quotations from Siecienski, Dvornik, Ware, Kriza, Alfeyev, Malmenvall, Geanakoplos, Syropoulos, Andrew of Santa Croce, Bessarion, John Eugenikos, and Bartholomew de Barberiis. After the Notaras removal I find no sentence that tracks any of those quotations closely enough to read as paraphrase-as-quotation. The two Ostroumoff paraphrases in the essay body are paraphrases of a public-domain 1861 text and are safe. No modernScholarship entry quotes anything; all of them describe. Please read the essay once more with the same question in mind, since this is a judgement call and a second reader is worth more than a second pass by the same one.

DOCTRINAL PARAGRAPH REWRITTEN, still needs clergy sign-off. The paragraph 'What Florence decided, and what had already been closed' previously stated flatly that constituting Father and Son as one principle gives the Son what belongs to the Father alone, and then asserted that an older Latin defence reading the phrase as manifestation and mission was set aside at Florence. Two problems. First, it stated our conclusion as though the Latin side agreed with the description of its own doctrine, which it does not. The paragraph now states the Orthodox conviction, states plainly that the Latin tradition denies its formula means this and why, states that Orthodox theology is not persuaded and why, and names it as a real disagreement. Second, the manifestation and mission claim came from the thread by way of Siecienski, could not be verified from any public-domain source in this session, and has been CUT from the essay entirely rather than shipped unverified. A priest should read the rewritten paragraph specifically for whether it states our position with enough force while describing the Latin position fairly.

POLEMIC CHECK. The source thread is hostile throughout: it calls the emperor God-accursed, calls the council a circus, and treats the whole affair as fraud. None of that survives. I re-read the essay looking for scoreboard sentences and cut the one that remained (Notaras). Nothing in this study attacks Oriental Orthodox or any other communion. The 449 material is handled as a case of bishops erring and being corrected, which is the point, not as an attack on anyone. The closing paragraph turns the warning back on ourselves. I judge the tone now within house standards, but tone is the reviewer's call.
NO EM DASHES. Checked every field of the returned object. None present. Ranges use hyphens (1438-1439, Acts 15:22-29).

estimatedMinutes CHANGED from 24 to 34. The draft's figure was inconsistent with the house scale. Measured against the shipped studies: theosis 918 words at 14 minutes, comma-johanneum 1168 at 20, papacy 2224 at 32, original-sin 2192 at 30, filioque 2235 at 35. This study runs roughly 2,650 words of essay plus florilegium, which places it above filioque. 34 is my estimate on that scale. Adjust if the reviewer reads the scale differently.

BIGGEST REMAINING GAP, unchanged and confirmed. There is still no quotation from St Mark of Ephesus. I searched the 1861 Ostroumoff scan specifically for direct quotation of Mark and found none: it discusses him at length and quotes him nowhere. The Encyclical Letter of 1440, the Confession of Faith, and the dying address to Bessarion circulate in English chiefly in the Holy Transfiguration Monastery translation, which is in copyright. A study on Florence with no words from Mark is a real weakness. If the reviewer can supply a pre-1929 English rendering, or authorise a fresh translation from the Greek by a competent translator, reopen the florilegium. In the meantime the app's existing mark-of-ephesus saint page should at least be linked from this study.

THE TWO OSTROUMOFF ENTRIES ARE STILL HISTORY, NOT PATRISTICS. Their glosses say so explicitly. The reviewer should decide whether a florilegium may carry a nineteenth-century historian at all, or whether these two belong in the essay body with the quotation marks dropped. Note also that Ostroumoff is a partisan Orthodox history, not a neutral chronicle, and that the archive.org title page credits A. V. Gorsky alongside Ostroumov, translator Vasilii Popov (anglicised Basil Popoff), editor J. M. Neale, publisher Joseph Masters, 1861. The item page does not print a place of publication, so 'London' has been dropped from the citation. If house style wants Gorsky named, add him.

OCR AND LIGATURE. The archive.org scan renders Joseph II's phrase as '(Ecumenical' where the printed page has 'Œcumenical'. I have set 'Œcumenical'. Confirm against the page image, and decide whether house style normalises it to 'Ecumenical'. This affects only the one florilegium entry.

LIMITS OF WHAT I COULD VERIFY IN OSTROUMOFF. I confirmed pp. 34 and 42. Everything the thread cites from later in the book, the bribes proposed by Dorotheus of Mitylene, the Greeks signing without reading the decree, non-voting members being made to sign, the count of patriarchal votes, the hollow kiss of peace, the impregnable fortress passage, is NOT quoted here and NOT asserted in the essay. If any of it matters to the argument, verify it in the printed 1861 text first and note that the thread's page numbers are from the 1971 reprint.

DATE STILL UNRESOLVED: the synod of Jerusalem at which the Patriarchs of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem rejected the union. This draft says 1443, which is the date in the standard reference works. The source thread, citing Alfeyev, says 1442. I did not resolve it. Confirm before ship.

DISPUTED EVENT, deliberately excluded. The thread cites a synod of Constantinople in 1450 that anathematised Florence and deposed Patriarch Gregory Mammas, and elsewhere mentions 1472. The acts of the supposed 1450 synod are treated by a number of historians, Gill among them, as a later fabrication. This study therefore rests the formal synodal annulment on the Constantinople synod of 1484 under Patriarch Symeon, which is not disputed. Confirm this is the line the reviewer wants, and whether 1450 should be mentioned at all, even as a disputed report.

PATRIARCH JOSEPH II. The essay says he died at Florence on 10 June 1439, before the decree was signed. Some accounts report a short written statement found among his papers after his death expressing agreement with the Latin position. That report is contested. Confirm the current formulation or add a clause acknowledging the disputed note. The florilegium gloss now also reports, from the same verified page, that Ostroumoff calls him old, weak, and undecided and says time proved him false to his own words; a reviewer may find that harsh on a dying man and want it softened.

WORDING KEPT ON PURPOSE. 'Of the Eastern bishops who remained to the end, Mark of Ephesus alone did not sign' is phrased that way because several bishops had died, left, or fled before the signing. The commoner formulation, 'Mark alone refused to sign', is less exact. Choose the wording you want.

NUMBERS NOT VERIFIED THIS RUN. 'Some four hundred bishops of the West' at Ariminum, and 'a few hundred men' reaching Constantinople in 1453. Both are round figures from the standard accounts. I verified from newadvent only that Ad Afros is the letter of ninety bishops of Egypt and Libya, which the essay and one gloss both assert; that one is confirmed.

DELIBERATELY OMITTED FROM THE THREAD, flagged in case the reviewer disagrees. CONSIDERED AND REJECTED, retained from the drafter's notes because I agree. Applying them to Florence would be an editorial stretch dressed as a canonical ruling. Flagging in case the reviewer disagrees.

STILL WANTED.
